english: In the autumn of the year renxu, just after the full moon of the seventh month, Master Su and his guest boated beneath the Red Cliff.
A clear breeze came gently, and the water stirred no ripple.
Raising wine, he toasted his guest, reciting the poem of the bright moon and singing the song of the Graceful One.
Soon the moon rose above the eastern mountain, lingering between the Dipper and the Ox constellations.
White dew spread over the river, and the gleam of water merged with the sky.
Let the reed of a boat drift wherever it would, over the boundless expanse of waters!
Vast indeed, it felt like riding the wind through void, knowing not where to stop;
floating light as if leaving the world and standing alone, becoming winged and rising to immortality.
Then, drinking with great joy, they beat the gunwale and sang.
The song ran: "O cinnamon oar, magnolia rudder, striking the moonlit void, we stem the gliding light;"
"far, far extends my longing; I gaze toward the Fair One at the sky's far end."
One of the guests played the dongxiao flute, keeping time with the song.
Its notes wailed mournfully, like resentment, like longing, like weeping, like complaint;
the lingering sound curling on, unbroken as a thread of silk.
It made the hidden dragon dance in the deep gorge, and drew tears from the widow alone in her boat.
Master Su grew sorrowful, straightened his robes and sat upright, and asked the guest: "Why does it sound so?"
The guest said: "'Bright the moon, sparse the stars, as southward fly the crows'—is this not the verse of Cao Mengde's strait at Zhou Yu's hands?
Westward one gazes at Xiakou, eastward at Wuchang; hills and streams interlace, sombrely deep—is this not where Mengde was hard pressed?

When he broke Jingzhou and took Jiangling, sailing east down the stream, his prows stretched a thousand li, banners veiling the sky, pouring wine on the river, lance athwart, chanting poems—he was truly the hero of an age; and where is he now?
Moreover, you and I fish and gather wood on the river islets, companion to fish and shrimp, friend to elk and deer, sailing a single leaf of a boat, raising gourd cups to toast one another.
We are mayflies lodged between heaven and earth, mere grains in the vast ocean.
I mourn the brevity of my life, and envy the endless Yangtze.
Would I fly with the immortals and roam, clasp the bright moon and endure forever.
Knowing this cannot suddenly be won, I entrust my lingering notes to the sorrowful wind.
Master Su said: "Do you too know, sir, the water and the moon?
The departing flows on like this, yet has never truly gone;
that which waxes and wanes like that, yet in the end neither lessens nor grows.
For if we view them from the side of change, heaven and earth cannot last even the blink of an eye;
if from the side of the unchanging, then all things and I are endless—so what is there to envy?
Moreover, between heaven and earth each thing has its owner; if it is not mine, though but a hair, I will not take it.
Only the clear breeze on the river and the bright moon between the hills, which the ear hears and makes sound, which the eye meets and makes colour—taking them none forbids, using them none exhausts.
These are the inexhaustible treasury of the Creator, which you and I may share.
The guest rejoiced and laughed; they rinsed the cups and poured again.
When the dainties were all consumed, cups and plates lay scattered in disarray.
Pillowed on one another in the boat, they knew not how the east grew light.
The Six Kings ended, the Four Seas became one; the Shu hills were stripped bare, and Epang Palace rose.
It covered more than three hundred li, shutting out the sky and the sun.
From Mount Li it stretched north, then bent west, running straight to Xianyang.
Two rivers flowed softly and poured into the palace walls.
Every five paces a tower, every ten paces a pavilion;
corridors wove like silk bands, eaves' teeth high-pecking like birds' beaks;
each hugging the terrain, interlocking at heart and butting horn to horn.
Coiling and swirling, like honeycombs and whirling water, the towers rose past counting into thousands and tens of millions.
The long bridge lay on the waves—without clouds, whence the dragon?
Sky-paths crossed the air—without rain clearing, whence the rainbow?
High and low bewildered the eye, one knew not east from west.
On the singing terraces warmth resounded, spring-like and mellow.
In the dancing halls cold sleeves stirred, stormy and chill.
Within a single day, within a single palace, the climate differed from place to place.
